era: After Chalcedon to the eve of the Reformation, 451 to 1516

nodes.name: Chalcedonian church
nodes.summary: Churches accepting Chalcedon confessed one Christ in two natures. Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches inherit this tradition, whose unity faced repeated disputes.
nodes.why: Catholic and Eastern Orthodox baptism and Eucharistic worship grew from a shared history before their medieval separation.
facts: They accept Christ as one person in two complete natures.
Rome and Constantinople remained major centers alongside the other patriarchal sees.
East and West developed different liturgies and approaches to authority.
The AD 1054 endpoint marks a gradual medieval separation.
nodes.sacraments: No universally fixed count. Baptism gives new birth. Eucharist gives Christ's body and blood. Confirmation, penance, ordination, marriage, and anointing develop. Seven becomes standard later.
nodes.today: Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches continue this inheritance. No separate membership.
nodes.disputed: Catholic and Orthodox churches each claim continuity with these churches. Neither describes itself as a new church founded in 1054.

nodes.name: Benedict of Nursia
nodes.summary: Benedict writes a rule for monks that shapes Western monasteries. Monks follow a shared pattern of prayer, work, obedience, and community life.
nodes.why: Monasteries sustain worship, learning, care for travelers, and Christian missions throughout medieval Europe.
facts: His life dates are approximate.
Tradition dates his move to Monte Cassino to about 529.
Christian monasticism already existed in Egypt, Palestine, and Asia Minor.
Monasteries following his rule preserve books and learning.

nodes.name: Constantinople II
nodes.summary: Emperor Justinian calls the fifth ecumenical council. It condemns the Three Chapters to clarify Chalcedon and seek reconciliation with Christians rejecting it.
nodes.why: Disagreements about Jesus continue after Chalcedon, and this council fails to reunite the divided churches.
facts: The Three Chapters concern Theodore of Mopsuestia and selected writings of Theodoret and Ibas.
The council affirms Christ as one person, fully divine and fully human.
Catholics and Eastern Orthodox accept this council.
The effort does not restore communion with the Oriental Orthodox churches.

nodes.name: Filioque dispute
nodes.summary: Western Christians add "and the Son" to the creed's account of the Holy Spirit. Eastern Christians dispute both the teaching and the alteration.
nodes.why: A short phrase becomes a lasting disagreement about the Trinity and who may change the church's creed.
facts: Filioque means "and the Son" in Latin.
Its use spreads in the West after Toledo in 589.
Rome first includes it in the creed during worship in 1014.
The dispute continues beyond this period of adoption.
nodes.disputed: Catholics defend the Latin teaching. Orthodox reject the unilateral change to the creed and generally reject its teaching about the Spirit's origin.

nodes.name: Gregory the Great
nodes.summary: Gregory leads the Roman church as pope, organizes relief, strengthens pastoral care, and sends monks to evangelize Anglo-Saxon England.
nodes.why: Gregory's relief work and missions help make bishops and monasteries central to daily life and Christianity's spread in Western Europe.
facts: 590 to 604 marks his papacy, not his lifespan.
A former Roman official, Gregory becomes a monk before becoming pope.
He sends Augustine of Canterbury and other monks to England.
His Pastoral Rule guides clergy in caring for their congregations.

nodes.name: Rise of Islam
nodes.summary: Islam arises in Arabia. Muslim armies conquer Syria, Palestine, Egypt, and much of North Africa. Ancient Christian centers come under Muslim rule.
nodes.why: Many early Christian homelands pass from Byzantine to Muslim rule, while their churches continue to worship.
facts: 622 marks Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina.
Byzantium loses Antioch, Jerusalem, and Alexandria to Muslim rule.
Christians continue worshiping under changing restrictions and conditions.
Conversions unfold over centuries, not immediately after conquest.

nodes.name: Constantinople III
nodes.summary: The sixth ecumenical council rejects monothelitism, the claim that Christ has one will. It affirms both his divine and human wills.
nodes.why: Christ's human will matters to the teaching that Jesus is fully human as well as fully divine.
facts: The council affirms two wills and two activities in one Christ.
Christ's human will freely follows his divine will.
It condemns Pope Honorius I among supporters of the rejected teaching.
Catholics and Eastern Orthodox accept this council.
nodes.disputed: Orthodox writers cite Honorius against papal infallibility. Catholics distinguish his condemned letters from an infallible papal definition.

nodes.name: Nicaea II
nodes.summary: The seventh ecumenical council permits honoring icons of Christ and the saints. It distinguishes veneration from worship owed to God.
nodes.why: This council gives Orthodox and Catholic Christians a basis for honoring sacred images in worship.
facts: Empress Irene supports the council against opponents of religious images.
Honor shown to an image refers to the person depicted.
This is the last council both Catholics and Eastern Orthodox generally accept as ecumenical.
Further conflict ends with the Byzantine restoration of icons in 843.
nodes.disputed: Many Protestants reject or restrict honoring religious images. Catholics and Orthodox distinguish this honor from worship of God.

nodes.name: Charlemagne crowned emperor
nodes.summary: Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne emperor in Rome on Christmas Day. The coronation ties the papacy to Frankish power and challenges Byzantine imperial claims.
nodes.why: Competing emperors and church alliances deepen the division between Rome and Constantinople.
facts: Charlemagne already rules the Franks.
The coronation creates a western rival to the emperor in Constantinople.
Frankish rulers support monasteries, church schools, and religious reforms.

nodes.name: Photian schism
nodes.summary: Rome and Constantinople break relations over Photius's appointment, church jurisdiction, and the Filioque. This temporary rupture anticipates the later East-West separation.
nodes.why: Papal authority and changes to the creed divide Rome and Constantinople long before 1054.
facts: Pope Nicholas I rejects Photius as patriarch in 863.
A Constantinople council condemns Nicholas and the Filioque in 867.
Ignatius's restoration ends the rupture in 867.
The 879 to 880 council later recognizes Photius as patriarch.
nodes.disputed: Catholic and Orthodox histories differ over responsibility, Photius's legitimacy, and which subsequent council deserves recognition.

nodes.name: Catholic church
nodes.summary: Churches in communion with the bishop of Rome develop as a distinct branch after the East-West separation, preserving apostolic succession and sacramental worship.
nodes.why: The Catholic branch is the setting for medieval councils and the later Protestant Reformation.
facts: 1054 marks a map division, not Catholicism's claimed founding date.
The pope holds universal authority in Catholic teaching.
The communion includes the Latin church and Eastern Catholic churches.
The Vatican reports 1.422 billion baptized Catholics for 2024.
nodes.sacraments: Seven sacraments convey grace. Baptism, including infants, brings new birth. Eucharistic bread and wine become Christ's body and blood through transubstantiation.
nodes.today: About 1.42 billion worldwide, especially the Americas, Europe, and Africa.

nodes.name: Eastern Orthodox churches
nodes.summary: Self-governing churches share Orthodox faith, bishops, liturgy, and sacramental communion. They honor Constantinople's patriarch as first among equals rather than a universal pope.
nodes.why: Eastern Orthodoxy shares roots and sacramental beliefs with Catholicism, while differing over papal authority. It is also distinct from Oriental Orthodoxy.
facts: 1054 marks a map division, not Orthodoxy's claimed founding date.
Greek, Russian, Romanian, and other churches belong to this tradition.
Orthodox churches accept the first seven ecumenical councils.
The population estimate excludes the separate Oriental Orthodox churches.
nodes.sacraments: Usually seven holy mysteries, though other rites also convey grace. Baptism, including infants, brings new birth. The Eucharist is truly Christ's body and blood.
nodes.today: Roughly 200 million, mainly Eastern Europe, Russia, and communities abroad.
nodes.disputed: Pew's 2010 figures imply about 208 million Eastern Orthodox. This rounded estimate is not a 2026 census.

nodes.name: Great Schism
nodes.summary: Roman legates and Constantinople's patriarch exchange excommunications. Their dispute becomes a conventional marker for the gradual separation of Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches.
nodes.why: Catholics and Eastern Orthodox remain divided despite sharing many beliefs about baptism and Communion.
facts: Disputes include papal authority, the Filioque, and worship customs.
The 1054 sentences target named church leaders, not every believer.
Paul VI and Athenagoras lift the mutual excommunications in 1965.
The 1965 gesture does not restore full communion.
nodes.disputed: Both traditions claim apostolic continuity and dispute responsibility for the split. Their separation developed over centuries.

nodes.name: Crusades
nodes.summary: Popes call military expeditions to the Holy Land. Crusaders establish Latin states, fight Muslim rulers, and sometimes attack Jewish communities and fellow Christians.
nodes.why: Crusading links warfare to penance, pilgrimage, and church authority. Its violence leaves lasting distrust between religious communities.
facts: Urban II calls the First Crusade in 1095.
Crusaders capture Jerusalem in 1099.
Church authorities offer penitential benefits to participants.
Acre falls in 1291. Other crusading campaigns continue elsewhere.

nodes.name: Waldensians
nodes.summary: Waldo's followers preach poverty and Scripture in ordinary language. Church authorities condemn their unauthorized preaching. The movement survives and later joins the Reformed tradition.
nodes.why: Calls for biblical preaching and church reform existed centuries before Luther.
facts: The approximate founding date is the 1170s in Lyon, France.
Both women and men preach in the medieval movement.
Waldensians join the Swiss Reformation in 1532.
Waldensian churches still exist in Italy and South America.
nodes.sacraments: Today, two sacraments are signs of grace. Baptism includes infants. Communion emphasizes Christ's spiritual presence. Medieval Waldensian views differed.
nodes.today: Tens of thousands, mainly Italy, Uruguay, and Argentina.
nodes.disputed: Medieval Waldensian communities did not all share the beliefs of modern Reformed churches.

nodes.name: Maronites and Rome
nodes.summary: Maronites formally confirm communion with Rome in 1182. They retain their Syriac liturgy within the Catholic communion.
nodes.why: Eastern Catholic churches share communion with the pope while keeping their own liturgical traditions.
facts: Maronites trace their spiritual roots to Saint Maron in the fourth and fifth centuries.
Their church develops in Syria and Lebanon.
They retain a West Syriac liturgical tradition.
Maronites form one church within today's Eastern Catholic family.
nodes.disputed: Maronites maintain that communion with Rome never broke. The 1182 date records confirmation, not an agreed founding or reunion.

nodes.name: Constantinople sacked
nodes.summary: Fourth Crusade armies sack Constantinople, loot churches, and impose Latin rule. The attack makes reunion with Rome far harder for Byzantine Christians.
nodes.why: The attack leaves Orthodox Christians with memories of violence and occupation that deepen their distrust of Rome.
facts: The attackers are Western Christians, not Muslim armies.
They plunder an Orthodox Christian capital.
A Latin empire and Latin patriarch replace Byzantine authorities.
Byzantines recover Constantinople in 1261, but distrust persists.
sources: Damick ch2: CLOSER YET FURTHER APART: THEOLOGY, LITURGICS, AND REUNION

nodes.name: Fourth Lateran Council
nodes.summary: Innocent III's council defines Eucharistic transubstantiation and requires annual confession and Easter Communion for believers who have reached the age of discernment.
nodes.why: Annual confession and Easter Communion become obligations for Western Christians. Transubstantiation becomes a focus of later Reformation debates.
facts: Transubstantiation names the change of bread and wine into Christ's body and blood.
Canon 21 requires confession at least once a year.
The same canon requires Communion at least at Easter.
Priests must keep confessions secret.
nodes.sacraments: The council defines transubstantiation and requires annual confession and Easter Communion. These rites already existed.

nodes.name: Thomas Aquinas
nodes.summary: Aquinas, a Dominican theologian, uses philosophy to explain Christian teaching. His Summa explains how sacraments convey grace and how bread and wine become Christ's body and blood.
nodes.why: His explanations shape Catholic sacramental language that Protestant reformers later debate.
facts: He writes the Summa Theologiae.
He teaches that sacraments receive their power from Christ.
Transubstantiation changes substance while bread and wine retain their observable properties.
He composes texts for Eucharistic worship.

nodes.name: Lyon II
nodes.summary: A profession of faith accepted at Lyon lists seven sacraments. Byzantine representatives agree to union with Rome, but the reunion fails to endure.
nodes.why: The formal list of seven sacraments classifies rites Christians already practiced.
facts: The list names baptism, confirmation, Eucharist, penance, orders, marriage, and anointing of the sick.
The profession also affirms transubstantiation.
Emperor Michael VIII supports reunion partly for political protection.
Opposition in the Byzantine church prevents lasting union.
nodes.sacraments: The profession of faith lists seven sacraments and affirms transubstantiation. Its count classifies older rites.
nodes.disputed: Catholics recognize Lyon II as ecumenical. Eastern Orthodox churches reject its authority and the attempted union.

nodes.name: Avignon papacy
nodes.summary: Seven successive popes base their court in Avignon rather than Rome. Strong French influence and a costly administration fuel criticism of papal leadership.
nodes.why: French influence and the cost of papal administration fuel distrust of church leadership before the Western Schism and Reformation.
facts: Clement V settles in Avignon in 1309.
Avignon becomes a major center of papal administration.
Gregory XI returns to Rome in January 1377.
The later rival Avignon popes belong to a separate crisis.

nodes.name: Western Schism
nodes.summary: Rival claimants in Rome and Avignon, later joined by Pisa, each claim the papacy. European rulers and churches divide their allegiance.
nodes.why: Rival popes weaken trust in Catholic leadership. The crisis ends without creating permanent denominational branches.
facts: Rival elections follow Gregory XI's death in 1378.
The Council of Pisa in 1409 adds a third claimant.
The Council of Constance resolves the main crisis.
Martin V's election in 1417 restores broad recognition of one pope.

nodes.name: Wycliffe and Lollards
nodes.summary: English church authorities condemn Wycliffe's teachings, including his rejection of transubstantiation. Lollard followers spread calls for biblical authority, preaching, and church reform.
nodes.why: Wycliffe challenges transubstantiation, and his followers press for biblical authority and church reform more than a century before Luther.
facts: 1382 marks condemnation, not the movement's beginning or end.
Wycliffe supports Scripture's authority over corrupt clergy.
His followers circulate English Scripture and criticize church wealth.
Lollard communities persist into the sixteenth century.
nodes.disputed: Wycliffe rejects transubstantiation but retains Christ's Eucharistic presence. Lollard beliefs vary, and some affirm more than a symbolic Communion.

nodes.name: Council of Constance
nodes.summary: The council ends the Western Schism by securing one recognized pope. It also condemns Jan Hus, whom secular authorities burn in 1415.
nodes.why: The council restores one recognized pope but condemns reformers, including Hus, whom secular authorities execute.
facts: The council elects Martin V in 1417.
It asserts council authority over popes in resolving the crisis.
It condemns Hus and hands him to secular authorities on July 6, 1415.
It also condemns Wycliffe's teachings.
nodes.sacraments: The council restricts the Eucharistic cup for laypeople, a practice contested by Hussites.
nodes.disputed: Catholics reject permanent council authority over popes. Many Protestants honor Hus as a reformer and reject his condemnation.

nodes.name: Hussite reform
nodes.summary: After Hus's execution, Bohemian reformers demand preaching, moral reform, and Communion in both bread and wine. War and negotiations produce several Hussite groups.
nodes.why: The Hussites make access to the Communion cup a central demand for church reform.
facts: Hussites take their name from Jan Hus.
Moderate Utraquists emphasize Communion under both bread and wine.
Radical groups hold differing doctrines and political aims.
The 1436 settlement does not end all Hussite traditions.
nodes.disputed: Hus did not adopt every teaching of Wycliffe. Later Hussite groups also differed from one another.

nodes.name: Council of Florence
nodes.summary: Eastern and Western delegates sign a reunion agreement in 1439. Most Orthodox communities reject it. A separate Armenian decree explains the seven sacraments.
nodes.why: Catholics inherit detailed sacramental teaching from this council, but its reunion agreement fails to overcome Orthodox opposition.
facts: The council moves from Ferrara to Florence in 1439.
The Greek agreement addresses the Filioque, purgatory, and papal primacy.
Mark of Ephesus refuses to sign the Greek union agreement.
The 1439 Armenian decree lists seven sacraments and describes their administration.
nodes.sacraments: The Armenian decree describes seven sacraments. Baptism brings new birth. Eucharistic bread and wine become Christ's body and blood. It specifies materials, words, and ministers.
nodes.disputed: Catholics accept the council as ecumenical. Orthodox churches reject it. Political pressure and opposition within Orthodox churches help explain the failed reunion.

nodes.name: Moscow rises
nodes.summary: Russian bishops elect their own metropolitan in 1448. Moscow's rulers expand their power and increasingly present their realm as a defender of Orthodox Christianity.
nodes.why: Moscow becomes a major Orthodox center as Byzantine power declines and Constantinople later falls.
facts: Jonah becomes metropolitan through an election by Russian bishops in 1448.
Moscow rejects the Florence reunion agreement.
Ivan III marries Byzantine princess Sophia Palaiologina in 1472.
The formal Moscow patriarchate begins later, in 1589.
nodes.disputed: Russian bishops elect their own metropolitan in 1448. Moscow becomes a patriarchate later. The explicit "Third Rome" claim chiefly dates to the sixteenth century.

nodes.name: Constantinople falls
nodes.summary: Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II captures Constantinople on May 29, ending the Byzantine Empire. Orthodox church life continues under Ottoman rule.
nodes.why: Orthodox churches lose Byzantine imperial protection and face the coming Reformation under Ottoman rule.
facts: Constantinople falls after a sustained Ottoman siege.
The Byzantine emperor Constantine XI dies during the capture.
The patriarchate survives under Ottoman authority.
Moscow grows in influence but does not replace every Orthodox center.

nodes.name: Unity of Brethren
nodes.summary: Reformers inspired by Hus organize the Unity of Brethren at Kunvald in Bohemia. This church is the historical ancestor of the Moravian tradition.
nodes.why: The Moravian church traces its roots to this medieval Bohemian reform movement, which it renews in the eighteenth century.
facts: Unitas Fratrum means Unity of Brethren.
The community begins in 1457, decades before Luther.
It emphasizes following Christ in daily life.
The later renewed Moravian church carries forward this tradition.
